name: Bessie Stringfield
story:
In 1930, a 19-year-old Black woman named Bessie Stringfield dropped a penny on a map of the United States, and wherever it landed, she rode. Alone on her Indian Scout motorcycle, she crossed all 48 continental states at a time when segregation meant she often couldn't find a motel that would take her. She slept on her bike at gas stations, survived on the kindness of Black families who opened their doors to a stranger, and kept riding.

When World War II broke out, Bessie volunteered as a civilian courier for the U.S. Army, carrying classified documents between domestic bases on her motorcycle — one of the few women, and the only Black woman, entrusted with the job. She completed the dangerous solo runs without incident, navigating back roads and hostile territories with nothing but nerve and a throttle.

After the war, she settled in Miami and became a local legend — racing in flat track competitions where she was often the only woman on the field and always the only Black competitor. When the city of Miami tried to ban her from riding on the causeway because of her race, she rode across it 'accidentally' so many times that the police gave up. She founded the Iron Horse Motorcycle Club, mentored young riders, and kept riding until she was in her sixties.

Bessie Stringfield never wrote a memoir or sought fame. She rode because the road was the one place where nobody could tell her she didn't belong. The American Motorcyclist Association later named their award for women in motorcycling after her — a quiet recognition that the woman they once ignored had been a pioneer all along.
